To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

‘The metabolic and evolutionary engineering of S. cerevisae for the anaerobic fermentation of plant biomass-derived carbon sources other than glucose, fructose, mannose and galactose has made significant progress, but further research is needed to enable the efficient conversion of industrial substrate mixtures.’

(i) the efficient anaerobic fermentation of xylose by S. cerevesiae is now possible, (ii) l-arabinose fermentation is also feasible, but still requires optimization and (iii) metabolic engineering of S. cerevisae for galacturonic and rhamnolactone fermentation is a promising but still challenging approach.

S. cerevisae can be genetically modified to ferment all major sugars present in plant biomass hydrolyzates, but that the fermentation of xylose, l-arabinose and galacturonic acids is still in its infancy and that the efficient conversion of these compounds into ethanol is still a major challenge.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of yeast strains that ferment all the major plant-derived carbon sources present in biomass hydrolysate, which is an important step towards the realization of a sustainable bioethanol economy.
the development of S. cerevisae strains that can ferment all of the major monosaccharide components of plant biomass hydrolysate to ethanol.
the construction of yeast strains that are able to ferment a wide range of plant biomass-derived sugars to ethanol.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current status of alcoholic fermentation of carbon sources from plant biomass hydrolyzates by S. cerevesiae is very promising and the future is bright.
S. cerevisae is a versatile organism that can be engineered to ferment most plant biomass-derived monomers into ethanol.

, despite the fact that the metabolic engineering of S. cerevisae for xylose fermentation has been successful, there is still a long way to go before the industrial implementation of the other strategies can be considered.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can ferment glucose and xylose, and that we have the potential to ferment galactose, arabinose, rhamnose and galacturonic acids.
the metabolic engineering of yeast strains for the efficient conversion of plant biomass hydrolysate components into ethanol is a very promising field, but it is still in its infancy.
the current status with regard to metabolic engineering of S. cerevisae strains that efficiently ferment the main plant biomass hydrolysate-derived monosac-charides is very promising.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the metabolic engineering of xylose and arabinose fermenting S. cerevisae strains is now well established.

the efficient fermentation of plant biomass hydrolysate by S. cereivisiae is feasible, but that the development of a commercial process will require further engineering of the yeast strain, the hydrolysate pretreatment process, and the fermentation process.
the metabolic engineering approach has already led to the development of yeast strains that can ferment the main monosaccharide components in plant biomass hydrolyzates.
